title: Longest Hiking Trail
statement:
A national park has **n** camps connected by **n - 1** two-way trails, and every camp can be reached from every other camp, so the trails form a tree. Trail i has length w kilometres.

The park wants to advertise its **longest possible hike**: the largest distance between two camps, where the distance is the total length of the (unique) path between them. Print this distance, known as the diameter of the tree.
input:
The first line contains an integer **n**.

Each of the next n - 1 lines contains three integers u, v and w: a trail of length w between camps u and v.
output: Print one integer: the diameter of the tree (0 if n = 1).

samples.explanation: The longest hike goes 3 → 2 → 4 → 5 with length 4 + 6 + 2 = 12.

hints: Checking the distances from every camp takes O(n^2) time: too slow.
Start anywhere and find the farthest camp x. Then the farthest camp from x is at distance equal to the diameter.
Use an explicit stack or queue instead of recursion: the tree can be a path of 10^5 camps. Distances need 64-bit integers.
editorial:
Two searches. First, from camp 1 compute distances to all camps (iterative DFS or BFS, adding trail lengths) and take the farthest camp x. One can prove that x is an end of some longest path. Second, compute distances from x; the largest one is the diameter. Each search is O(n).

Alternatively, a single DFS can keep for every vertex the two longest downward paths; the best sum over all vertices is the diameter.

Complexity: O(n).
